articles.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
articles.summary: The origin of the seeds used in ECDSA, one of the most widely used cryptographic standards, has been revealed. Claude, a researcher at Anthropic, discovered that the seeds were generated using the lrand48 random-number generator, which samples bytes from the RNG initialized by a Unix timestamp. This is a surprising finding, as the seeds were previously thought to be the result of a hash algorithm. The discovery sheds light on the cryptographic community's understanding of the seed values, which had been a long-standing mystery.

articles.title: The Decoherence Trap: When AI slop drowns out the signal in an endless sea of noise
articles.summary: Decoherence grows relative to the rate of change of a system, leading to runaway exponential growth and limiting the rate at which a system can improve outside of its decoherent state. This phenomenon is not new, but the widespread use of AI is currently producing it at a rate that is unsustainable. The good news is that this rules out the specter of runaway recursive self-improvement, but the bad news is that we are barreling toward a different kind of disaster known as Decoherence Collapse, where the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible models within a system leads to a catastrophic collapse of the system's coherence.

This is mitigated by TPMs having endorsement keys and certificates, which can be verified by a list of legitimate vendors and their CA keys. However, if the TPM is less accessible, such as mounted directly to the motherboard or inside the CPU, it can be trickier to bypass, but a USB-to-SPI bridge can be used to connect an easily available TPM module.
